title: Async/Await and Typed Promises
summary: Type async functions and the promises they return, run work at the same time, put time limits on it, and stream values with async generators.
intro: Programs spend a lot of their time waiting: for a database, a file, or another service. JavaScript represents each wait with a promise, and TypeScript types the value the promise will hold, so whatever you get from `await` is fully typed. In this lesson you type async functions, run several at once, give slow work a time limit with `AbortSignal`, and read data that arrives a page at a time. The examples wait with `sleep` from `node:timers/promises`, a real timer kept short.

steps.title: Promise<T> and async functions

examples.title: Load a user
examples.prompt: Load a user from a fake database that takes 10 ms to answer, and build a greeting from it in a second async function.
examples.explanation: `loadUser` returns `Promise<User>`, so `await loadUser(id)` gives a `User`, as the first bubble shows, and `user.email` type-checks. `greeting` returns a template string, so its return type is `Promise<string>`. The callback you pass to `then` receives the value inside the promise, so `text` is a `string` with no annotation. A `throw` inside an async function doesn't escape as an exception: it rejects the promise, which is how `loadUser` reports an id it doesn't know.

examples.title: Forgetting await
examples.prompt: Load a user and print its name, but leave out the `await`.
examples.output: main.ts(11,28): error TS2339: Property 'name' does not exist on type 'Promise<User>'.
examples.explanation: Without `await`, `user` is the promise itself, a `Promise<User>`, and a promise has no `name` property. Plain JavaScript would run this and print `Hello, undefined`. The checker stops it before it runs, and the message names the type you're really holding. The fix is one word: `const user = await loadUser(1);`.

examples.title: Top-level await
examples.prompt: Load two users, one after the other, at the top level of the file, and log each step.
examples.output:
loading user 1
loaded Ada
loading user 2
loaded Grace
done
examples.explanation: Every `await` here sits at the top level of the module, with no `async function main()` around it, which an ES module allows. The file waits at each `await` until that promise settles, so the second load starts only after the first one finishes, and the lines print in the order the code is written. Two 10 ms loads take about 20 ms this way. The next part starts independent work at the same time instead.

practice.title: Price lookup
practice.prompt:
Add up a cart with a price service that takes a moment to answer.

1. Make `getPrice` async, with the return type `Promise<number | undefined>`. Wait 5 ms with `await sleep(5)`, then return the SKU's price in cents from `PRICES`, which is `undefined` for an unknown SKU.
2. Make `total` async, with the return type `Promise<number>`. Await the price of each SKU, add up the ones that exist, and skip unknown SKUs.
3. Print the cart's total in dollars with 2 decimals.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `getPrice` and `total` from your file.

Expected output:

```text
Total: $30.48
```

cases.name: the total is a promise until you await it

hints: Put `async` before `function`, and write the return type after the parameters, like `loadUser(id: number): Promise<User>` in the examples.
In `getPrice`, `await sleep(5);` pauses first, and `return PRICES.get(sku);` resolves the promise with the price or `undefined`.
In `total`, loop with `for (const sku of skus)`, write `const price = await getPrice(sku);`, and add `price` to the sum only when `price !== undefined`.

steps.title: Running promises together

examples.title: Load a page's data at once
examples.prompt: Load a user and their orders at the same time with `Promise.all`, and log each load as it finishes.
examples.output:
orders loaded
user loaded
Ada: 2 orders, $17.49
examples.explanation: Both loads start at once, so the pair takes about 30 ms instead of 40. The orders finish first, as the log shows, but `Promise.all` keeps the input order: the user comes first in the result because `loadUser(1)` comes first in the array. The bubble shows the tuple `[User, Order[]]`, so destructuring gives `user` and `orders` their own types with no annotations.

examples.title: An optional widget fails
examples.prompt: Load three dashboard widgets with `Promise.allSettled`, and show the one that fails as unavailable instead of failing the whole page.
examples.output:
weather: 12°C and cloudy
news: unavailable (news service timed out)
quote: Make it work, then make it fast.
examples.explanation: `Promise.allSettled` waits for all three widgets, so the failing news widget doesn't take the others down with it. Each result is a `PromiseSettledResult<string>`, a union tagged by `status`. After `result.status === "fulfilled"`, the bubble shows the fulfilled member, which has `value`. The rejected member has `reason` instead, typed `any`, because a promise can reject with anything. So `show` checks it with `instanceof Error`, just like a caught error, before it reads `message`.

examples.title: race and any
examples.prompt: Ask three mirrors for the same file, where the fastest one is down, and compare what `Promise.race` and `Promise.any` give you.
examples.output:
race failed: eu is down
any: us
examples.explanation: `mirrors()` starts three fresh requests for each call. `Promise.race` settles with whichever promise settles first, and that's the `eu` mirror failing at 10 ms, so the race rejects. `Promise.any` skips failures and waits for the first success, `us` at 30 ms. Both return a `Promise<string>` here, so `winner` is a `string`. When every promise rejects, `Promise.any` rejects with an `AggregateError`, which the Error Handling with Types lesson covers.

practice.title: Dashboard
practice.prompt:
Load what a dashboard shows at the same time, and keep the page working when its optional part fails.

1. Load the profile, the orders, and the notifications with one `Promise.all`, and destructure the three results.
2. Load the recommendations with `Promise.allSettled`. They always fail here.
3. Print the four lines below. The orders line shows how many orders there are and their total in dollars.
4. Print `recommendations: ` followed by the titles joined with `, ` when they load, and `recommendations: unavailable` when they don't.

Expected output:

```text
profile: Ada (pro)
orders: 2, total $43.98
notifications: 3 unread
recommendations: unavailable
```

tests.output:
profile: Ada (pro)
orders: 2, total $43.98
notifications: 3 unread
recommendations: unavailable

hints: `const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([...])` gives each result its own type, in the order you list the calls.
`Promise.allSettled([loadRecommendations()])` resolves to a one-item tuple, so destructure it with `const [recommendations] = ...`.
Check `recommendations.status === "fulfilled"` before you read `recommendations.value`. The other branch prints `recommendations: unavailable`.

steps.title: Timeouts with AbortSignal

examples.title: A timed-out sleep
examples.prompt: Give a quick wait and a slow wait their own time limit, and print what happens to each.
examples.output:
quick: done after 10 ms
slow: AbortError after 50 ms
examples.explanation: Each call makes its own `AbortSignal.timeout`. The quick wait ends long before its 200 ms limit, so `sleep` resolves normally. The slow one would take a whole second, but its signal aborts at 50 ms, and `sleep` rejects right then with an `AbortError`, so the program never waits out the second. The `catch` variable is `unknown`, as always, so the code checks `instanceof Error` before it reads `name`.

examples.title: Passing a signal through
examples.prompt: Build a report in four steps with a 200 ms limit, checking the signal before each step.
examples.output:
finished load rows
finished add totals
finished render PDF
report stopped: TimeoutError
examples.explanation: `buildReport` takes the signal as a parameter and checks it before every step. The limit passes while the PDF renders, but nothing interrupts that step, because `sleep(step.ms)` wasn't given the signal. The next check, before emailing, finds the signal aborted, and `throwIfAborted` throws its reason, a `TimeoutError`. Pass the signal into each step as well, as `sleep(step.ms, undefined, { signal })`, and the render itself stops at 200 ms with an `AbortError`.

examples.title: A withTimeout helper
examples.prompt: Write a generic `withTimeout` that hands work a signal and turns a timeout into a value you can check, then use it on a fast and a slow stock lookup.
examples.output:
fast: 12
slow: gave up after 100 ms
examples.explanation: `withTimeout` makes the signal, hands it to the work, and turns an abort into the string `"timeout"`. The return type `Promise<T | "timeout">` puts that outcome in the type, so `fast` is `number | "timeout"`, as the bubble shows, and code has to rule out `"timeout"` before it treats a result as a number, as the `else` branch does before it calls `toFixed`. Any other error is a real failure, and since `signal.aborted` is still `false` for it, it's rethrown. Write `return await` inside `try`: a plain `return work(signal)` hands back the promise before it settles, and its rejection skips this `catch`.

practice.title: Slow services
practice.prompt:
Give two services a 50 ms time limit, and report which one answered in time.

1. Export `withTimeout<T>(work: (signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<T>, ms: number): Promise<T | "timeout">`. It runs `work` with a signal that aborts after `ms` milliseconds, and resolves to `"timeout"` when that signal aborted.
2. Rethrow any error that isn't a timeout.
3. For each service, call `withTimeout` with work that runs `ping(service, signal)` and a 50 ms limit. Print `<name>: <result>`.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `withTimeout` from your file.

Expected output:

```text
fast: ok
slow: timeout
```

cases.name: resolves to the work's type or timeout
a timeout is a possible result
the work receives the signal
cases.code: const r: boolean | "timeout" = await withTimeout(async (signal) => signal.aborted, 10);

cases.name: the limit is a number of milliseconds

hints: Make the signal first with `const signal = AbortSignal.timeout(ms);`, then call `work(signal)` inside `try`, as `withTimeout` does in the last example.
Write `return await work(signal);` so a rejection lands in your `catch`. There, return `"timeout"` when `signal.aborted` is `true`, and `throw err` otherwise.
In the loop, `await withTimeout((signal) => ping(service, signal), 50)` resolves to `ok` or `timeout`, ready to print.

steps.title: Async generators and for await

examples.title: Countdown
examples.prompt: Count down from 3 with a pause before each number, then lift off.
examples.explanation: `countdown` waits 10 ms before each number, then yields it. Its return type `AsyncGenerator<number>` says every yielded value is a number, so `n` in the loop is a `number`, as the bubble shows, and a `yield "three"` inside would be TS2322. `for await` asks for the next number only after the loop body has run, and the loop ends when the generator's own loop does, so `liftoff` prints last.

examples.title: Pages, stopped early
examples.prompt: Search a product catalog that arrives one page at a time, and stop as soon as you find the cup.
examples.output:
fetching page 1
checking MUG-01
checking TEA-02
fetching page 2
checking CUP-03
found the cup: CUP-03
examples.explanation: The generator fetches a page only when the loop needs its first product, which is why `fetching page 2` prints after the products of page 1. The cup is on page 2, and `break` stops the generator there, so page 3 is never fetched. Pages from a real API work the same way: the loop reads as if the whole catalog were an array, and you only pay for the pages you use.

examples.title: Collect with Array.fromAsync
examples.prompt: Collect every product from the same paged catalog into arrays, once whole and once mapped to SKUs.
examples.output:
5 products: Mug, Teapot, Cup, Pot, Jug
MUG-01, TEA-02, CUP-03, POT-04, JUG-05
examples.explanation: `Array.fromAsync` reads a generator to the end and resolves to an array, typed `Product[]` because the generator is an `AsyncGenerator<Product>`. Its optional second argument maps each value as it arrives, so the second call resolves to a `string[]`. Collecting is the simplest way to read everything, but it waits for every page and holds them all in memory. Use `for await` when you can handle values one at a time or might stop early.

practice.title: Paginated reader
practice.prompt:
Read every fruit from a paged API with an async generator that follows its cursors.

1. Export `readAll(fetchPage: (cursor: string | null) => Promise<Page<string>>): AsyncGenerator<string>` as an `async function*`.
2. Fetch the first page with the cursor `null`, and yield each of its items. Then fetch the page that `nextCursor` names, and keep going until `nextCursor` is `null`.
3. Print every fruit from `readAll(fetchFruit)` with `for await`, one per line. `fetchFruit` logs each fetch itself, so a lazy reader prints those lines between the fruits.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `readAll` from your file.

Expected output:

```text
fetch first page
apple
banana
fetch p2
cherry
fetch p3
damson
elderberry
```

tests.output:
fetch first page
apple
banana
fetch p2
cherry
fetch p3
damson
elderberry

cases.name: is an async generator of strings
cases.code: const g: AsyncGenerator<string> = readAll(async () => ({ items: [], nextCursor: null }));

cases.name: yields strings, not numbers
cases.code: const g: AsyncGenerator<number> = readAll(async () => ({ items: [], nextCursor: null }));

cases.name: works with for await
cases.code: for await (const item of readAll(async () => ({ items: ["a"], nextCursor: null }))) { const s: string = item; }

hints: Keep the cursor in a variable that starts as `null`, the cursor of the first page: `let cursor: string | null = null;`.
Loop: `const page = await fetchPage(cursor);`, `yield` each item of `page.items`, then stop when `page.nextCursor` is `null`, or set `cursor` to it and go around again.
Print with `for await (const fruit of readAll(fetchFruit))`. Each fetch line lands between the fruits because a page is fetched only when the loop asks for its first item.

recap:
- An `async` function returns `Promise<T>`, and `await` unwraps it to a `T`. Forget `await`, and the checker reports that you're holding a promise.
- `main.ts` is an ES module, so `await` works at the top level.
- `Promise.all` runs promises at once and resolves to a typed tuple in input order. It rejects on the first failure.
- `Promise.allSettled` never rejects. Narrow each result by `status`, and treat `reason`, typed `any`, like a caught error.
- `Promise.race` settles like the first promise to settle, and `Promise.any` resolves with the first success.
- `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` aborts after a delay. Pass a `signal` to APIs that take one, and call `signal.throwIfAborted()` between steps of your own.
- An `async function*` returns `AsyncGenerator<T>`. Read it with `for await`, stop it with `break`, or collect it with `Array.fromAsync`.
